# Lua API walkthrough

<!-- Generated by scripts/docs/generate_lua_api.py; edit website/api.json. -->

Every supported public builtin has a common call shape, explanation, and
example below. Square brackets in signatures mark optional arguments; they
are not Lua syntax. Examples are small fragments unless they define a whole
callback, and asset-dependent examples require the named/numbered assets.

Read the [language and project reference](reference.md) for the Lua subset,
16:16 numbers, callbacks, source modules, and input mapping. The
[renderer contract](render-modes.md) defines exact accepted Mode 0 call shapes
and AUTO fallback conditions; a common signature here is not a promise that
every argument expression can use Mode 0. Audio v2 does not support PCM
`sample`; use the [four-channel audio API](audio/api-v2.md).

## Input

### btn

```text
btn(index)
```

Check whether a button is held down.

Indices: 0 left, 1 right, 2 up, 3 down, 4 B, 5 A, 6 Start, 7 Select, 8 L, 9 R. Invalid indices return false. In the editor preview, Z is A and X is B.

```lua
if btn(0) then x -= 2 end
```

### btnp

```text
btnp(index)
```

React to a button press, with held-button repeat.

Fires on held tick 1, then 15, 19, 23, and every four held ticks thereafter. Releasing resets the counter. Use btn() for continuous movement.

```lua
if btnp(5) then score = 0 end
```

## Sprites and poses

### spr

```text
spr(id, x, y [, w, h, flip_x, flip_y])
```

Draw a cell or rectangle from the shared sprite sheet.

Use spr for shared-sheet tiles and simple sheet-based objects, especially artwork also used by a map. Sprite cells are 8×8 pixels. Position is the top-left corner; width and height are in cells. Color 0 is transparent by default. Create the artwork in Sprite Lab → Shared Tiles first. If an object's tile layout and offsets should be reusable editor assets, draw an authored pose with pspr. If it should play an ordered sequence of poses, use anim.

```lua
spr(1, 112, 72)
```

### sspr

```text
sspr(sx, sy, sw, sh, dx, dy [, dw, dh, flip_x, flip_y])
```

Draw a rectangular part of the sprite sheet.

Source coordinates and sizes are in pixels. Scaling or arbitrary crops require the bitmap renderer; aligned, unscaled rectangles may use hardware sprites.

```lua
sspr(8, 0, 8, 8, 112, 72)
```

### pspr

```text
pspr(name_or_id, x, y [, flip_x [, flip_y]])
```

Draw one authored pose: a reusable image assembled from tiles.

Use pspr for a static character frame, prop, effect, or UI element whose tile layout and offsets belong in Sprite Lab rather than repeated Lua spr calls. A pose may combine several tile parts; pspr draws that one pose and does not advance frames. Use anim for a timed pose sequence. Register hero_idle in Sprite Lab → Poses first, then use COPY LUA CALL. Prefer a case-sensitive literal pose name: the build resolves it to the current index with no runtime lookup or name storage. Other poses can be deleted or reordered without changing the call. Missing literal names fail the build with a source position and a close spelling suggestion when available. Names must be string literals, optionally parenthesized; dynamic string lookup and generated symbols are not supported. Existing zero-based numeric IDs still work, but deletion shifts later IDs. Out-of-range numeric literals emit nonfatal build warnings after normal 16:16 conversion; invalid dynamic numeric IDs draw nothing. The origin and offsets come from the recipe; flips mirror within its calculated tile bounds. Poses use objsheet.json when present, otherwise the shared sheet. Mode 0 still requires a proven working set and hardware resource budgets; choosing a pose alone does not guarantee eligibility.

```lua
function _draw()
  cls(0)
  pspr("hero_idle", 100, 60)
end
```

### anim

```text
anim(name, x, y [, flip_x [, flip_y [, elapsed_seconds]]])
```

Draw a timed sequence of poses using an authored animation clip.

Use anim for walking, flying, pickups, attacks, or other ordered pose sequences: the editor owns the frame order, FPS, and loop setting instead of Lua frame-index arithmetic. Use pspr for one static pose. Register idle in Sprite Lab → Animations before building. Without elapsed_seconds, calls use the shared game clock and identical clips stay synchronized. Switching the clip name does not restart it: anim is stateless. For an action or independent entity, store started when the action begins and supply time() - started; do not reset started every draw. Negative elapsed time selects the first frame; nonlooping clips hold their final frame. Flips use a fixed rectangle across every pose in the clip. Unknown literal names fail the build; unknown dynamic names or empty clips draw nothing. No entity or playback state is allocated.

```lua
function _draw()
  cls(0)
  anim("idle", 100, 60)
end
```

### pvariant

```text
pvariant() / pvariant(name_or_id)
```

Select a named color variant for subsequent pose and animation draws.

Create alternate in Sprite Lab → Poses → Color Variants. Variants are project-wide simultaneous palette-index replacements; index 0 remains transparent. They affect pspr and anim, not spr or maps, and remain active across frames until reset. Numeric IDs are 1-based; prefer names when editing the library. Unknown literal names fail builds; unknown dynamic names/IDs reset original colors. Mode 0 may share 4bpp pixels with separate hardware palettes; Mode 4 compiles recolored artwork. Exact resource and call-shape restrictions are in the renderer contract.

```lua
pvariant("alternate")
anim("idle", 100, 60)
pvariant() -- restore original colors
```

### sget

```text
sget(x, y)
```

Read a palette index from the sprite sheet.

This reads authored sheet pixels, not the finished screen.

```lua
pixel = sget(8, 0)
```

### sset

```text
sset(x, y, color)
```

Change a pixel in the sprite sheet.

This changes the game’s runtime copy. It does not save artwork back to your project. Hardware rendering requires bounded mutation placement; see the renderer contract.

```lua
sset(8, 0, 40)
```

### fget

```text
fget(id [, flag])
```

Read a sprite’s flags.

With a flag index, reads that bit; without it, returns the flag byte. Flags are useful for labeling solid or collectible tiles.

```lua
solid = fget(1, 0)
```

### fset

```text
fset(id, flags) / fset(id, flag, value)
```

Change a sprite’s flags.

A flag affects the logical sprite and later map filtering. Runtime mutation can change AUTO renderer selection.

```lua
fset(1, 0, true)
```

## Maps

### map

```text
map() / map(bg [, cx, cy, x, y, w, h, mask])
```

Draw the tile maps you created in the editor.

map() draws all authored non-empty planes, back to front. With arguments, the first is always a literal BG0–BG3 layer. Do not mix automatic and explicit forms. Source-cell offsets contribute to world positions; read the map contract before scrolling a subsection.

```lua
function _draw()
  cls(24)
  map()
  spr(1, 112, 72)
end
```

### mget

```text
mget(x, y) / mget(bg, x, y)
```

Read the sprite ID in a map cell.

Map coordinates are in 8×8 cells. The two-argument form uses BG0. Invalid coordinates or absent planes return 0.

```lua
tile = mget(3, 4)
```

### mset

```text
mset(x, y, id) / mset(bg, x, y, id)
```

Replace a map cell while the game runs.

The three-argument form edits BG0. Runtime edits are not saved into project files. Invalid coordinates are ignored.

```lua
mset(3, 4, 2)
```

### camera

```text
camera([x, y])
```

Move the view without moving your game objects.

The camera position is subtracted from drawing coordinates. camera() resets the view. Keep world coordinates separate from screen coordinates.

```lua
camera(120, 0)
```

## Drawing

### cls

```text
cls([color])
```

Clear the screen for a new frame.

Colors are palette indices. In Aurora, 24 is dark blue and 15 is white. Put one unconditional cls() at the start of _draw() for hardware-renderer eligibility.

```lua
function _draw()
  cls(24)
  print("HELLO GBA", 8, 8, 15)
end
```

### print

```text
print(text, x, y, color)
```

Draw text or a number on the screen.

This explicit four-argument form is the easiest to start with. Separate labels and numeric values to keep them eligible for hardware rendering. Text uses a 6×8 cell font; Mode 0 has additional glyph and object limits.

```lua
print("COINS", 8, 8, 15)
print(5, 56, 8, 15)
```

### pset

```text
pset(x, y [, color])
```

Set one screen pixel.

Screen coordinates start at (0, 0) in the top-left. The screen is 240 pixels wide and 160 high.

```lua
pset(120, 80, 40)
```

### pget

```text
pget(x, y)
```

Read a color from the composed screen.

The result reflects drawing that has already happened. Use sget() to inspect the sprite sheet instead.

```lua
pixel = pget(120, 80)
```

### line

```text
line(x0, y0, x1, y1 [, color])
```

Draw a straight line between two points.

The current camera and clipping rectangle apply to the line.

```lua
line(16, 16, 100, 80, 15)
```

### rect

```text
rect(x0, y0, x1, y1 [, color])
```

Draw a rectangle outline.

The last two coordinates are the opposite corner, not width and height. The endpoints are inclusive.

```lua
rect(32, 40, 96, 80, 17)
```

### rectfill

```text
rectfill(x0, y0, x1, y1 [, color])
```

Draw a filled rectangle.

Use opposite-corner coordinates. Drawing a filled rectangle is a bitmap-renderer operation.

```lua
rectfill(32, 40, 96, 80, 17)
```

### circ

```text
circ(x, y, radius [, color])
```

Draw a circle outline.

The first two coordinates are the center. The radius is measured in pixels.

```lua
circ(120, 80, 16, 40)
```

### circfill

```text
circfill(x, y, radius [, color])
```

Draw a filled circle.

Useful for quick prototypes and particles; this selects bitmap rendering.

```lua
circfill(120, 80, 16, 40)
```

### color

```text
color([index])
```

Set the default drawing color.

Explicit color arguments override the default. cls() does not change it.

```lua
color(40)
```

### cursor

```text
cursor([x, y, color])
```

Set the text cursor position and optional color.

Explicitly positioned print() calls are usually clearer for a first game.

```lua
cursor(8, 8, 15)
```

### clip

```text
clip() / clip(x, y, width, height)
```

Limit drawing to a rectangle.

clip() restores full-screen drawing. Smaller clipping rectangles require Mode 4 in the current hardware-renderer subset.

```lua
clip(16, 16, 208, 128)
```

### pal

```text
pal() / pal(bank) / pal(source, replacement [, bank])
```

Remap one palette color to another.

Bank 0 (default) remaps subsequent drawing; bank 1 remaps the displayed palette, including already drawn pixels. pal(bank) resets that bank. pal() resets both banks and restores default transparency. Only banks 0 and 1 are supported. Mode 0 imposes placement and remapping restrictions; see the renderer contract.

```lua
pal(40, 17)
```

### palt

```text
palt() / palt(color, transparent)
```

Control which sprite colors are transparent.

The default makes palette index 0 transparent in sprites and maps. Arbitrary transparent colors require Mode 4.

```lua
palt(0, true)
```

## Audio

### sfx

```text
sfx(id [, priority])
```

Play a short sound-effect clip.

Create an SFX clip with this ID in Audio first, or use Coin Quest’s included clip 0. Default priority is 160. sfx(-1) stops gameplay-owned effects.

```lua
sfx(0)
```

### music

```text
music(id)
```

Start a song from the Audio workspace.

Create a song with this ID first. music(-1) stops song-owned notes while leaving gameplay effects independent.

```lua
music(0)
```

### gba_note

```text
gba_note(channel, note, sound_id [, duration_ticks])
```

Play a hardware note using a saved sound.

Channels are 1–4. The sound must match the channel. Timed notes use 96 ticks per quarter note; zero duration sustains until stopped.

```lua
gba_note(1, 72, 0, 24)
```

### gba_stop

```text
gba_stop(channel)
```

Stop notes on a hardware channel.

Use channel numbers 1–4. This is a direct channel command; music and effects share these hardware channels.

```lua
gba_stop(1)
```

## Math and bit operations

### flr

```text
flr(number)
```

Round down to an integer.

flr(-1.5) is -2, not -1. Use it when converting pixel coordinates into map cells.

```lua
tile_x = flr(19 / 8)
```

### ceil

```text
ceil(number)
```

Round up to an integer.

ceil(-1.5) is -1. Numbers in mTile use 16:16 fixed point.

```lua
pages = ceil(17 / 8)
```

### abs

```text
abs(number)
```

Get the distance of a number from zero.

abs(-8) is 8. Handy for simple collision checks.

```lua
distance = abs(24 - 112)
```

### sgn

```text
sgn(number)
```

Return -1 for a negative number, or 1 otherwise.

sgn(0) returns 1.

```lua
direction = sgn(-3)
```

### min

```text
min(a, b)
```

Choose the smaller of two numbers.

Use this to cap a value at an upper limit.

```lua
health = min(health + 1, 5)
```

### max

```text
max(a, b)
```

Choose the larger of two numbers.

Use this to keep a value above a lower limit.

```lua
health = max(health - 1, 0)
```

### mid

```text
mid(a, b, c)
```

Choose the middle value of three numbers.

Putting a value between its lower and upper bounds clamps it to that range.

```lua
x = mid(8, x, 224)
```

### sin

```text
sin(turns)
```

Get the vertical sine component of a turn.

Angles use turns, not degrees or radians. sin(0.25) is -1, matching a screen where Y increases downward.

```lua
y = 80 + sin(0.25) * 16
```

### cos

```text
cos(turns)
```

Get the horizontal cosine component of a turn.

One complete turn is 1. cos(0) is 1.

```lua
x = 120 + cos(0) * 16
```

### atan2

```text
atan2(dx, dy)
```

Find a direction angle in turns.

Uses the screen-coordinate convention shared with sin() and cos().

```lua
angle = atan2(1, 0)
```

### sqrt

```text
sqrt(number)
```

Find a square root.

Zero and negative inputs return 0. Fixed-point precision is finite; squared distances can avoid square roots when comparing distances.

```lua
distance = sqrt(3 * 3 + 4 * 4)
```

### rnd

```text
rnd([limit])
```

Choose a pseudorandom fixed-point number.

The numeric form ranges from zero up to, but excluding, a positive limit. rnd() uses a limit of 1; a zero or negative limit returns 0. Table-item selection is not implemented: choose an index with flr(rnd(#items)) + 1 for a nonempty list.

```lua
roll = flr(rnd(6)) + 1
```

### srand

```text
srand(seed)
```

Set the random-number seed.

A fixed seed makes random sequences repeatable for testing.

```lua
srand(42)
```

### band

```text
band(a, b)
```

Bitwise AND.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = band(6, 3)
```

### bor

```text
bor(a, b)
```

Bitwise OR.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = bor(4, 1)
```

### bxor

```text
bxor(a, b)
```

Bitwise exclusive OR.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = bxor(6, 3)
```

### bnot

```text
bnot(number)
```

Invert the bits of a number.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = bnot(0)
```

### shl

```text
shl(a, b)
```

Shift bits left.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = shl(1, 2)
```

### shr

```text
shr(a, b)
```

Shift bits right with sign extension.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = shr(8, 1)
```

### lshr

```text
lshr(a, b)
```

Shift bits right without sign extension.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = lshr(8, 1)
```

### rotl

```text
rotl(a, b)
```

Rotate bits left.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = rotl(1, 2)
```

### rotr

```text
rotr(a, b)
```

Rotate bits right.

These operate on the 32-bit fixed-point representation. Keep bit operations separate from ordinary arithmetic until you are comfortable with that representation.

```lua
bits = rotr(4, 2)
```

## Tables and strings

### add

```text
add(table, value [, index])
```

Append or insert a value into a list.

Lua list indices start at 1. Insertion shifts the existing elements.

```lua
coins = {}
add(coins, 40)
```

### del

```text
del(table, value)
```

Remove the first matching value from a list.

Searches the contiguous list first and shifts it when removing an item; if no list match exists, also searches named/hash entries. Returns the removed value, or nil when absent. Use deli() to remove by list index.

```lua
coins = {10, 20, 30}
del(coins, 20)
```

### deli

```text
deli(table [, index])
```

Remove an element by its list index.

With no index, removes the final element.

```lua
coins = {10, 20, 30}
deli(coins, 2)
```

### count

```text
count(table [, value])
```

Count the list prefix or matching table values.

Without a value (or with nil), returns the contiguous numbered length, stopping at the first nil. With a non-nil value, counts matches across occupied array and hash slots, including named fields.

```lua
coins = {1, 2, 1}
total = count(coins, 1)
```

### all

```text
for value in all(table) do ... end
```

Visit each value in a list.

all() is iterator syntax here. Do not assign the iterator itself to a variable.

```lua
total = 0
for value in all({10, 20, 30}) do
  total += value
end -- total is 60
```

### pairs

```text
for key, value in pairs(table) do ... end
```

Visit a table’s keys and values.

Do not rely on a particular traversal order.

```lua
total = 0
for key, value in pairs({score=5}) do
  total += value
end -- total is 5
```

### foreach

```text
foreach(table, callback)
```

Call a function for each list element.

Use a named, statically bound callback. Read the foreach guide for mutation rules.

```lua
total = 0
function accumulate(value)
  total += value
end
foreach({10, 20}, accumulate) -- total is 30
```

### sub

```text
sub(text, first [, last])
```

Take a section of a string.

Indices start at 1 and the final index is inclusive. String operations are byte-oriented.

```lua
name = sub("EXPLORER", 1, 4)
```

### tostr

```text
tostr(value [, hex])
```

Convert a value to text.

For Mode 0 text, print numeric values directly instead of passing a converted string.

```lua
label = tostr(42)
```

### tonum

```text
tonum(text)
```

Convert numeric text to a number.

Invalid or nonnumeric input returns nil; test the result before arithmetic. Numeric input is returned unchanged.

```lua
speed = tonum("2.5")
```

### chr

```text
chr(code)
```

Create a one-byte string from a character code.

65 is uppercase A. This is a byte operation, not a Unicode conversion.

```lua
letter = chr(65)
```

### ord

```text
ord(text [, index])
```

Read a byte’s numeric character code.

Indices start at 1. An index outside the string returns nil.

```lua
code = ord("GBA", 1)
```

## Time and diagnostics

### time

```text
time()
```

Read elapsed game time in seconds.

t() is an alias. This is game time, not the computer’s wall clock.

```lua
seconds = time()
```

### t

```text
t()
```

Read elapsed game time in seconds.

An alias for time().

```lua
seconds = t()
```

### stat

```text
stat(id)
```

Read runtime performance counters.

stat(1) is the previous tick’s share of the roughly 30 Hz frame budget: 1 means the entire budget. It is not host CPU percentage. See the performance guide for other counters.

```lua
load = stat(1)
```

### printh

```text
printh(value [, filename])
```

Accept a compatibility call without producing output.

Currently a no-op in compiled games and the editor ROM preview. Arguments are evaluated, but no console log or file is written. Use print() in _draw() to display a value on screen.

```lua
printh("coin collected")
```
